label.reasoning: The item tests the direct relationship between hydrogen bonding and water’s high specific heat. Recognizing that added heat disrupts intermolecular hydrogen bonds before substantially increasing molecular motion requires recall of a single concept.

The item tests recognition that hydrogen bonding between water molecules accounts for water’s high specific heat. Choice A directly states this relationship; no multistep reasoning or additional unit content is required.

The item directly tests enzyme catalysis: complementary substrate binding at the active site lowers activation energy. Selecting this description requires recognition of a core enzyme principle, without applying it to a new situation or performing multi-step reasoning.

The item directly tests enzyme-substrate specificity and how enzymes lower activation energy (EK 3.1.A.1–2). Selecting D requires recognition of these basic enzyme properties, without application or multi-step reasoning.

Students apply the distinction between passive and active transport to the concentration data. Entry from 5 mM outside to a higher concentration inside would move X against its concentration gradient, supporting active transport (choice B). This requires one conceptual application rather than simple recall.

Students apply the distinction between passive and active transport to a concentration gradient. Movement of X into the cell from 5 mM outside to a higher concentration inside is against the gradient, supporting active transport (choice B). Knowing whether a membrane protein carried X is unnecessary.

The item applies Mendelian segregation and dominance to a monohybrid cross. Crossing Pp with pp produces equal proportions of Pp (purple) and pp (white), so half the offspring are expected to have white flowers.

Students must recognize that the recessive phenotype represents homozygous recessive individuals, then apply Hardy-Weinberg equations: q² = 0.16, q = 0.4, p = 0.6, and 2pq = 0.48. This applies one population-genetics model rather than combining distinct mechanisms.

The item applies natural selection to heritable color variation under changing environmental conditions. Dark beetles experience less predation, increasing their reproductive success and the frequency of dark-color alleles over generations (choice B). It requires applying one concept to reach a single conclusion.

The item applies natural selection to heritable color variation under predation pressure. Dark beetles are better camouflaged, increasing their survival and reproductive success; consequently, dark-color alleles become more frequent over generations. This requires applying one concept to the described environment.
